entries.02173af6514ecf3e4394233620226e64819885d5: <div sID="gen32433" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="1Tim.5" sID="1Tim.5"/> <div eID="gen32433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32434" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32435" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle, I. Directs Timothy how to reprove, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.1-1Tim.5.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. Adverts to widows, both elder and younger, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.3-1Tim.5.16">ver. 3-16</reference>. III. To elders, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17-1Tim.5.19">ver. 17-19</reference>. IV. Treats of public reproof, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.20">ver. 20</reference>. V. Gives a solemn charge concerning ordination, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.21-1Tim.5.22">ver. 21, 22</reference>. VI. Refers to his health (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.23">ver. 23</reference>), and states men's sins to be very different in their effects, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.24-1Tim.5.25">ver. 24, 25</reference>.
entries.6c8c73f002d508c509668b01dc9a3146f47fd846: <div eID="gen32435" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32434" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Directions Concerning Reproofs. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32436" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Rebuke not an elder, but intreat <hi type="italic">him</hi> as a father; <hi type="italic">and</hi> the younger men as brethren; <hi type="super">2</hi> The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity. <div eID="gen32436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32437" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle gives rules to Timothy, and in him to other ministers, in reproving. Ministers are reprovers by office; it is a part, though the least pleasing part, of their office; they are to preach the word, to reprove and rebuke, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.2">2 Tim. iv. 2</reference>. A great difference is to be made in our reproofs, according to the age, quality, and other circumstances, of the persons rebuked; thus, and elder in age or office must be entreated as a father; <hi type="italic">on some have compassion, making a difference,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.22">Jude 22</reference>. Now the rule is, 1. To be very tender in rebuking elders—elders in age, elders by office. Respect must be had to the dignity of their years and place, and therefore they must not be rebuked sharply nor magisterially; but Timothy himself, though an evangelist, must entreat them as fathers, for this would be the likeliest way to work upon them, and to win upon them. 2. The younger must be rebuked as brethren, with love and tenderness; not as desirous, to spy faults or pick quarrels, but as being willing to make the best of them. There is need of a great deal of meekness in reproving those who deserve reproof. 3. The elder women must be reproved, when there is occasion, as mothers. <reference osisRef="Hos.2.2">Hos. ii. 2</reference>, <hi type="italic">Plead with your mother, plead.</hi> 4. The younger women must be reproved, but reproved as <hi type="italic">sisters, with all purity.</hi> If Timothy, so mortified a man to this world and to the flesh and lusts of it, had need of such a caution as this, much more have we.
entries.7274f55698a8b57e1f2434a4d93ca0d8ac6b4ea0: <div eID="gen32437" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Directions Concerning Widows. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32438" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Honour widows that are widows indeed. <hi type="super">4</hi> But if any widow have children or nephews, let them learn first to show piety at home, and to requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God. <hi type="super">5</hi> Now she that is a widow indeed, and desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day. <hi type="super">6</hi> But she that liveth in pleasure is dead while she liveth. <hi type="super">7</hi> And these things give in charge, that they may be blameless. <hi type="super">8</hi> But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel. <hi type="super">9</hi> Let not a widow be taken into the number under threescore years old, having been the wife of one man, <hi type="super">10</hi> Well reported of for good works; if she have brought up children, if she have lodged strangers, if she have washed the saints' feet, if she have relieved the afflicted, if she have diligently followed every good work. <hi type="super">11</hi> But the younger widows refuse: for when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry; <hi type="super">12</hi> Having damnation, because they have cast off their first faith. <hi type="super">13</hi> And withal they learn <hi type="italic">to be</hi> idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not. <hi type="super">14</hi> I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house, give none occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully. <hi type="super">15</hi> For some are already turned aside after Satan. <hi type="super">16</hi> If any man or woman that believeth have widows, let them relieve them, and let not the church be charged; that it may relieve them that are widows indeed. <div eID="gen32438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32439" type="x-p"/> Directions are here given concerning the taking of widows into the number of those who were employed by the church and had maintenance from the church: <hi type="italic">Honour widows that are widows indeed.</hi> Honour them, that is, maintain them, admit them into office. There was in those times an office in the church in which widows were employed, and that was to tend the sick and the aged, to look to them by the direction of the deacons. We read of the care taken of widows immediately upon the first forming of the Christian church (<reference osisRef="Acts.6.1">Acts vi. 1</reference>), where the Grecians thought their widows were neglected in the daily ministration and provision made for poor widows. The general rule is to <hi type="italic">honour widows that are widows indeed,</hi> to maintain them, to relieve them with respect and tenderness. <div eID="gen32439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32440" type="x-p"/> I. It is appointed that those widows only should be relieved by the charity of the church who were pious and devout, and not wanton widows that <hi type="italic">lived in pleasure,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.5-1Tim.5.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. She is to be reckoned a widow indeed, and it to be maintained at the church's charge, who, being <hi type="italic">desolate, trusteth in God.</hi> Observe, It is the duty and comfort of those who are desolate to trust in God. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> God sometimes brings his people into such straits that they have nothing else to trust to, that they may with more confidence trust in him. Widowhood is a desolate estate; but <hi type="italic">let the widows trust in me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.11">Jer. xlix. 11</reference>), and rejoice that they have a God to trust to. Again, Those who trust in God must <hi type="italic">continue in prayer.</hi> If by faith we confide in God, by prayer we must give glory to God and commit ourselves to his guidance. Anna was a widow indeed, who <hi type="italic">departed not from the temple</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.37">Luke ii. 37</reference>), <hi type="italic">but served God with fasting and prayer night and day.</hi> But she is not a widow indeed <hi type="italic">that lives in pleasure</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.6">v. 6</reference>), or who lives licentiously. A jovial widow is not a widow indeed, not fit to be taken under the care of the church. <hi type="italic">She that lives in pleasure is dead while she lives,</hi> is no living member of the church, but as a carcase in it, or a mortified member. We may apply it more generally; those who live in pleasure are dead while they live, spiritually dead, <hi type="italic">dead in trespasses and sins;</hi> they are in the world to no purpose, buried alive as to the great ends of living. <div eID="gen32440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32441" type="x-p"/> II. Another rule he gives is that the church should not be charged with the maintenance of those widows who had relations of their own that were able to maintain them. This is mentioned several times (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">If any widow have children or nephews,</hi> that is grandchildren or near relations, let them maintain them, and let not the church be burdened. So <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.16">v. 16</reference>. This is called showing <hi type="italic">piety at home</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.4">v. 4</reference>), or showing piety towards their own families. Observe, The respect of children to their parents, with their care of them, is fitly called piety. This is requiting their parents. Children can never sufficiently requite their parents for the care they have taken of them, and the pains they have taken with them; but they must endeavour to do it. It is the indispensable duty of children, if their parents be in necessity, and they in ability to relieve them, to do it to the utmost of their power, <hi type="italic">for this is good and acceptable before God.</hi> The Pharisees taught that a gift to the altar was more acceptable to God than relieving a poor parent, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.5">Matt. xv. 5</reference>. But here we are told that this <hi type="italic">is better than all burnt-offerings and sacrifices; this is good and acceptable,</hi> &c. He speaks of this again (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.8">v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">If any provide not for his own,</hi> &c. If any men or women do not maintain their own poor relations who belong to them, they do in effect <hi type="italic">deny the faith;</hi> for the design of Christ was to confirm the law of Moses, and particularly the law of the fifth commandment, which is, <hi type="italic">Honour thy father and mother;</hi> so that those deny the faith who disobey that law, much more if they provide not for their wives and children, who are parts of themselves; if they spend that upon their lusts which should maintain their families, they have denied the faith <hi type="italic">and are worse than infidels.</hi> One reason why this care must be taken that those who are rich should maintain their poor relations, and not burden the church with them is (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.16">v. 16</reference>) <hi type="italic">that it may relieve those who are widows indeed.</hi> Observe, Charity misplaced is a great hindrance to true charity; there should be prudence in the choice of the objects of charity, that it may not be thrown away upon those who are not properly so, that there may be the more for those who are real objects of charity. <div eID="gen32441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32442" type="x-p"/> III. He gives directions concerning the characters of the widows that were to be taken into the number to receive the church's charity: not under sixty years old, nor any who have divorced their husbands or been divorced from them and have married again; she must have been <hi type="italic">the wife of one man,</hi> such as had been a housekeeper, had a good name for hospitality and charity, <hi type="italic">well reported of for good works.</hi> Observe, Particular care ought to be taken to relieve those, when they fall into decay, who, when they had wherewithal, were ready to every good work. Here are instances of such good works as are proper to be done by good wives: <hi type="italic">If she have brought up children:</hi> he does not say, If she have borne children (<hi type="italic">children are a heritage of the Lord</hi>), that depends on the will of God; but, if she had not children of her own, yet if she had brought up children. <hi type="italic">If she have lodged strangers,</hi> and <hi type="italic">washed the saints' feet;</hi> if she have been ready to give entertainment to good Christians and good ministers, when they were in their travels for the spreading of the gospel. Washing of the feet o their friends was a part of their entertainments. <hi type="italic">If she have relieved the afflicted</hi> when she had ability, let her be relieved now. Observe, Those who would find mercy when they are in distress must show mercy when they are in prosperity. <div eID="gen32442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32443" type="x-p"/> IV. He cautions them to take heed of admitting into the number those who are likely to be no credit to them (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The younger widows refuse:</hi> they will be weary of their employments in the church, and of living by rule, as they must do; so they <hi type="italic">will marry, and cast off their first faith.</hi> You read of a first love (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.4">Rev. ii. 4</reference>), and here of a first faith, that is, the engagements they gave to the church to behave well, and as became the trust reposed in them: it does not appear that by their first faith is meant their vow not to marry, for the scripture is very silent on that head; besides the apostle here advises the younger widows to marry (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.14">v. 14</reference>), which he would not if hereby they must have broken their vows. Dr. Whitby well observes, "If this faith referred to a promise made to the church not to marry, it could not be called their first faith." <hi type="italic">Withal they learn to be idle, and not only idle, but tattlers,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.13">v. 13</reference>. Observe, It is seldom that those who are idle are idle only, they learn <hi type="italic">to be tattlers and busy-bodies,</hi> and to make mischief among neighbours, and sow discord among brethren. Those who had not attained to such a gravity of mind as was fit for the deaconesses (or the widows who were taken among the church's poor), let them <hi type="italic">marry, bear children,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.14">v. 14</reference>. Observe, If housekeepers do not mind their business, but are tattlers, they give occasion to the adversaries of Christianity to reproach the Christian name, which, it seems, there were some instances of, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.15">v. 15</reference>. We learn hence, 1. In the primitive church there was care taken of poor widows, and provision made for them; and the churches of Christ in these days should follow so good an example, as far as they are able. 2. In the distribution of the church's charity, or alms, great care is to be taken that those share in the public bounty who most want it and best deserve it. A widow was not to be taken into the primitive church that had relations who were able to maintain her, or who was not well reported of for good works, but lived in pleasure: <hi type="italic">But the younger widows refuse, for, when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry.</hi> 3. The credit of religion, and the reputation of Christian churches, are very much concerned in the character and behaviour of those that are taken into any employment in the church, though of a lower nature (such as the business of deaconesses), or that receive alms of the church; if they do not behave well, but are tatlers and busy-bodies, they will give occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully. 4. Christianity obliges its professors to relieve their indigent friends, particularly poor widows, that the church may not be charged with them, that it may relieve those that are widows indeed: rich people should be ashamed to burden the church with their poor relations, when it is with difficulty that those are supplied who have no children or nephews, that is, grand-children, who are in a capacity to relieve them.
entries.7f6725f4a49940d5359956d5808063fa7e5ec934: <div eID="gen32443" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Directions Concerning Elders; Concerning Church Discipline. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32444" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine. <hi type="super">18</hi> For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer <hi type="italic">is</hi> worthy of his reward. <hi type="super">19</hi> Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses. <hi type="super">20</hi> Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear. <hi type="super">21</hi> I charge <hi type="italic">thee</hi> before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels, that thou observe these things without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality. <hi type="super">22</hi> Lay hands suddenly on no man, neither be partaker of other men's sins: keep thyself pure. <hi type="super">23</hi> Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities. <hi type="super">24</hi> Some men's sins are open beforehand, going before to judgment; and some <hi type="italic">men</hi> they follow after. <hi type="super">25</hi> Likewise also the good works <hi type="italic">of some</hi> are manifest beforehand; and they that are otherwise cannot be hid. <div eID="gen32444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32445" type="x-p"/> Here are directions, <div eID="gen32445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32446" type="x-p"/> I. Concerning the supporting of ministers. Care must be taken that they be honourably maintained (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour</hi> (that is, of double maintenance, double to what they have had, or to what others have), <hi type="italic">especially those who labour in the word and doctrine,</hi> those who are more laborious than others. Observe, The presbytery ruled, and the same that ruled were those <hi type="italic">who laboured in the word and doctrine:</hi> they had not one to preach to them and another to rule them, but the work was done by one and the same person. Some have imagined that by the <hi type="italic">elders that rule well</hi> the apostle means lay-elders, who were employed in ruling but not in teaching, who were concerned in church-government, but did not meddle with the administration of the word and sacraments; and I confess this is the plainest text of scripture that can be found to countenance such an opinion. But it seem a little strange that mere ruling elders should be accounted worthy of double honour, when the apostle preferred preaching to baptizing, and much more would he prefer it to ruling the church; and it is more strange that the apostle should take no notice of them when he treats of church-officers; but, as it is hinted before, they had not, in the primitive church, one to preach to them and another to rule them, but ruling and teaching were performed by the same persons, only some might labour more in the word and doctrine than others. Here we have, 1. The work of ministers; it consists principally in two things: ruling well and labouring in the word and doctrine. This was the main business of elders or presbyters in the days of the apostles. 2. The honour due to those who were not idle, but laborious in this work; they were worthy of double honour, esteem, and maintenance. He quotes a scripture to confirm this command concerning the maintenance of ministers that we might think foreign; but it intimates what a significancy there was in many of the laws of Moses, and particularly in this, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treads out the corn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.25.4">Deut. xxv. 4</reference>. The beasts that were employed in treading out the corn (for that way they took instead of threshing it) were allowed to feed while they did the work, so that the more work they did the more food they had; therefore let the elders that labour in the word and doctrine be well provided for; <hi type="italic">for the labourer is worthy of his reward</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.10">Matt. x. 10</reference>), and there is all the reason in the world that he should have it. We hence learn, (1.) God, both under the law, and now under the gospel, has taken care that his ministers be well provided for. Does God take care for oxen, and will he not take care of his own servants? The ox only treads out the corn of which they make the bread that perishes; but ministers break the bread of life which endures for ever. (2.) The comfortable subsistence of ministers, as it is God's appointment that those who preach the gospel should live of the gospel (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.14">1 Cor. ix. 14</reference>), so it is their just due, as much as the reward of the labourer; and those who would have ministers starved, or not comfortably provided for, God will require it of them another day. <div eID="gen32446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32447" type="x-p"/> II. Concerning the accusation of ministers (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses.</hi> Here is the scripture-method of proceeding against an elder, when accused of any crime. Observe, 1. There must be an accusation; it must not be a flying uncertain report, but an accusation, containing a certain charge, must be drawn up. Further, He is not to be proceeded against by way of enquiry; this is according to the modern practice of the inquisition, which draws up articles for men to purge themselves of such crimes, or else to accuse themselves; but, according to the advice of Paul, there must be an accusation brought against an elder. 2. This accusation is not to be received unless supported by two or three credible witnesses; and the accusation must be received before them, that is, the accused must have the accusers face to face, because the reputation of a minister is, in a particular manner, a tender thing; and therefore, before any thing be done in the least to blemish that reputation, great care should be taken that the thing alleged against him be well proved, that he be not reproached upon an uncertain surmise; "but (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.20">v. 20</reference>) <hi type="italic">those that sin rebuke before all;</hi> that is, thou needest not be so tender of other people, but rebuke them publicly." Or "those that sin before all rebuke before all, that the plaster may be as wide as the wound, and that those who are in danger of sinning by the example of their fall may take warning by the rebuke given them for it, <hi type="italic">that others also may fear.</hi>" Observe, (1.) Public scandalous sinners must be rebuked publicly: as their sin has been public, and committed before many, or at least come to the hearing of all, so their reproof must be public, and before all. (2.) Public rebuke is designed for the good of others, that they may fear, as well as for the good of the party rebuked; hence it was ordered under the law that public offenders should receive public punishment, that <hi type="italic">all Israel</hi> might <hi type="italic">hear, and fear, and do no more wickedly.</hi> <div eID="gen32447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32448" type="x-p"/> III. Concerning the ordination of ministers (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lay hands suddenly on no man;</hi> it seems to be meant of the ordaining of men to the office of the ministry, which ought not to be done rashly and inconsiderately, and before due trial made of their gifts and graces, their abilities and qualifications for it. Some understand it of absolution: "Be not too hasty in laying hands on any; remit not the censure of the church to any, till time be first taken for the proof of their sincerity in their repentance, <hi type="italic">neither be partakers of other men's sins,</hi> implying that those who are too easy in remitting the censures of the church encourage others in the sins which are thus connived at, and make themselves thereby guilty." Observe, We have great need to watch over ourselves at all times, that we do not make ourselves partakers of other men's sins. "Keep thyself pure, not only from doing the like thyself, but from countenancing it, or being any way accessary to it, in others." Here is, 1. A caution against the rash ordination of ministers, or absolution of those who have been under church-censures: <hi type="italic">Lay hands suddenly on no man.</hi> 2. Those who are rash, either in the one case or the other, will make themselves partakers in other men's sins. 3. We must keep ourselves pure, if we will be pure; the grace of God makes and keeps us pure, but it is by our own endeavours. <div eID="gen32448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32449" type="x-p"/> IV. Concerning absolution, to which <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.24-1Tim.5.25">v. 24, 25</reference>, seem to refer: <hi type="italic">Some men's sins are open beforehand, going before to judgment, and some follow after,</hi> &c. Observe, Ministers have need of a great deal of wisdom, to know how to accommodate themselves to the variety of offences and offenders that they have occasion to deal with. Some men's sins are so plain and obvious, and not found by secret search, that there is no dispute concerning the bringing of them under the censures of the church; they <hi type="italic">go before to judgment,</hi> to lead them to censure.—<hi type="italic">Others they follow after;</hi> that is, their wickedness does not presently appear, nor till after a due search has been made concerning it. Or, as some understand it, some men's sins continue after they are censured; they are not reformed by the censure, and in that case there must be no absolution. So, also, as to the evidences of repentance: <hi type="italic">The good works of some are manifest beforehand. And those that are otherwise,</hi> whose good works do not appear, their wickedness <hi type="italic">cannot be hid,</hi> and so it will be easy to discern who are to be absolved, and who are not. Observe, 1. There are secret, and there are open sins; some men's sins are open beforehand, and going unto judgment, and some they follow after. 2. Sinners must be differently dealt with by the church. 3. The effects of church-censures are very different; some are thereby humbled and brought to repentance, so that their good works are manifest beforehand, while it is quite otherwise with others. 4. The incorrigible cannot be hid; for God will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and make manifest the counsels of all hearts. <div eID="gen32449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32450" type="x-p"/> V. Concerning Timothy himself. 1. Here is a charge to him to be careful of his office; and a solemn charge it is: <hi type="italic">I charge thee before God, as thou wilt answer it to God before the holy and elect angels, observe these things without partiality,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.21">v. 21</reference>. Observe, It ill becomes ministers to be partial, and to have respect of persons, and to prefer one before another upon any secular account. He charges him, by all that is dear, <hi type="italic">before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels,</hi> to guard against partiality. Ministers must give an account to God and the Lord Jesus Christ, whether, and how, they have observed all things given them in charge: and woe to them if they have been partial in their ministrations, out of an worldly politic view. 2. He charges him to take care of his health: <hi type="italic">Drink no longer water,</hi> &c. It seems Timothy was a mortified man to the pleasures of sense; he drank water, and he was a man of no strong constitution of body, and for this reason Paul advises him to use wine for the helping of his stomach and the recruiting of his nature. Observe, It is a little wine, for ministers must not be given to much wine; so much as may be for the health of the body, not so as to distemper it, for God has made wine to rejoice man's heart. Note, (1.) It is the will of God that people should take all due care of their bodies. As we are not to make them our masters, so neither our slaves; but to use them so that they may be most fit and helpful to us in the service of God. (2.) Wine is most proper for sickly and weak people, whose stomachs are often out of order, and who labour under infirmities. <hi type="italic">Give strong drink to him that is ready to perish, and wine to those that are of heavy hearts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.6">Prov. xxxi. 6</reference>. (3.) Wine should be used as a help, and not a hindrance, to our work and usefulness.  <chapter eID="1Tim.5"/> <div eID="gen32450" type="x-p"/>

entries.a7e93e07e9a1176b2c48328c21bc75f25ad33996: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18123"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <div sID="gen37336" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.1-1Tim.5.25">1Ti 5:1-25</reference>. General Directions as to How Timothy Should Deal with Different Classes in the Church.<div eID="gen37336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37337" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18123"/><hi type="bold">1. an elder--</hi>in age; probably not an elder in the ministry; these latter are not mentioned till <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17">1Ti 5:17</reference>, "the elders that rule." Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.2.17">Ac 2:17</reference>, "your old men," literally, "elders." Contrasted with "the younger men." As Timothy was admonished so to conduct himself as to give no man reason to despise his youth (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Ti 4:12</reference>); so here he is told to bear in mind his youth, and to behave with the modesty which becomes a young man in relation to his elders.<div eID="gen37337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37338" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Rebuke not--</hi>literally, "Strike not hard upon"; Rebuke not sharply: a different word from "rebuke" in <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.2">2Ti 4:2</reference>.<div eID="gen37338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37339" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">entreat--</hi>exhort.<div eID="gen37339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37340" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as brethren--</hi>and therefore equals; not lording it over them (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.1-1Pet.5.3">1Pe 5:1-3</reference>). <div eID="gen37340" type="x-p"/>
entries.735f374e62b0d38dabc1848a33afea3ecbdddf1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18124"/><div sID="gen37341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18124"/><hi type="bold">2. with all purity--</hi>respectful treatment of the other sex will promote "purity." <div eID="gen37341" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e587ca74d7c628c690f64a36ad2164439fa1eed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18125"/><div sID="gen37342" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18125"/><hi type="bold">3. Honour--</hi>by setting on the church roll, as fit objects of charitable sustenance (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.9">1Ti 5:9</reference>, 17, 18; <reference osisRef="Acts.6.1">Ac 6:1</reference>). So "honor" is used for support with necessaries (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.4">Mt 15:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.28.10">Ac 28:10</reference>).<div eID="gen37342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37343" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">widows indeed--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.16">1Ti 5:16</reference>). Those really desolate; not like those (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.4">1Ti 5:4</reference>) having children or relations answerable for their support, nor like those (in <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.6">1Ti 5:6</reference>) "who live in pleasure"; but such as, from their earthly desolation as to friends, are most likely to trust wholly in God, persevere in continual prayers, and carry out the religious duties assigned to Church widows (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.5">1Ti 5:5</reference>). Care for widows was transferred from the Jewish economy to the Christian (<reference osisRef="Deut.14.29">De 14:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.16.11">16:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.24.17">24:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.24.19">19</reference>). <div eID="gen37343" type="x-p"/>
entries.683755e58466a73a56717d3be5dab7ca7e54d27c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18126"/><div sID="gen37344" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18126"/><hi type="bold">4. if any widow have children--</hi>not "a widow indeed," as having children who ought to support her.<div eID="gen37344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37345" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nephews--</hi>rather, as Greek, "descendants," or "grandchildren" [Hesychius]. "Nephews" in old English meant "grandchildren" [Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, 5.20].<div eID="gen37345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37346" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let them--</hi>the children and descendants.<div eID="gen37346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37347" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">learn first--</hi>ere it falls to the Church to support them.<div eID="gen37347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37348" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to show piety at home--</hi>filial piety towards their widowed mother or grandmother, by giving her sustenance. Literally, "to show piety towards their own house." "Piety is applied to the reverential discharge of filial duties; as the parental relation is the earthly representation of God our heavenly Father's relation to us. "Their own" stands in opposition to the Church, in relation to which the widow is comparatively a stranger. She has a claim on her own children, prior to her claim on the Church; let them fulfil this prior claim which she has on them, by sustaining her and not burdening the Church.<div eID="gen37348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">parents--</hi>Greek, (living) "progenitors," that is, their mother or grandmother, as the case may be. "Let them learn," implies that abuses of this kind had crept into the Church, widows claiming Church support though they had children or grandchildren able to support them.<div eID="gen37349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37350" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good and--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit. The words are probably inserted by a transcriber from <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.3">1Ti 2:3</reference>. <div eID="gen37350" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e7cdd2d5994887d665f7aa58d652ab6a14ec226: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18127"/><div sID="gen37351" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18127"/><hi type="bold">5. widow indeed, and desolate--</hi>contrasted with her who has children or grandchildren to support her (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.4">1Ti 5:4</reference>).<div eID="gen37351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trusteth in God--</hi>perfect tense in Greek, "hath rested, and doth rest her hope in God." <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.5">1Ti 5:5</reference> adds another qualification in a widow for Church maintenance, besides her being" desolate" or destitute of children to support her. She must be not one "that liveth in pleasure" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.6">1Ti 5:6</reference>), but one making God her main hope (the accusative in Greek expresses that God is the ultimate aim whereto her hope is directed; whereas, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.10">1Ti 4:10</reference>, dative expresses hope resting on God as her present stay [Wiesinger]), and continuing constantly in prayers. Her destitution of children and of all ties to earth would leave her more unencumbered for devoting the rest of her days to God and the Church (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.33">1Co 7:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.34">34</reference>). Compare also "Anna a widow," who remained unmarried after her husband's death and "departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers day and night" (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.36">Lu 2:36</reference>, 37). Such a one, Paul implies, would be the fittest object for the Church's help (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.3">1Ti 5:3</reference>); for such a one is promoting the cause of Christ's Church by her prayers for it. "Ardor in prayers flows from hoping confidence in God" [Leo].<div eID="gen37352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in supplications and prayers--</hi>Greek, "in her supplications and prayers"; the former signifies asking under a sense of need, the latter, prayer (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1">1Ti 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">Php 4:6</reference>).<div eID="gen37353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37354" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">night and day--</hi>another coincidence with Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.7">Lu 18:7</reference>, "cry day and night"); contrast Satan's accusations "day and night" (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.10">Re 12:10</reference>). <div eID="gen37354" type="x-p"/>
entries.1fbc6f8b7b0b53197ef221ca6f526239445713da: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18128"/><div sID="gen37355" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18128"/><hi type="bold">6. she that liveth in pleasure--</hi>the opposite of such a widow as is described in <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.5">1Ti 5:5</reference>, and therefore one utterly undeserving of Church charity. The Greek expresses wanton prodigality and excess [Tittmann]. The root expresses weaving at a fast rate, and so lavish excess (see on <reference osisRef="Jas.5.5">Jas 5:5</reference>).<div eID="gen37355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dead while she liveth--</hi>dead in the Spirit while alive in the flesh (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.22">Mt 8:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">Ep 5:14</reference>). <div eID="gen37356" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0a077c5691f5947671ab7f43c8201ce22f99a6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18129"/><div sID="gen37357" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18129"/><hi type="bold">7. these things--</hi>just now spoken (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.5">1Ti 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.6">6</reference>).<div eID="gen37357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37358" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they may be blameless--</hi>namely, the widows supported by the Church. <div eID="gen37358" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7b9fc1fc21d6b967d8e0a3f50840dbf7bb8ed9c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18130"/><div sID="gen37359" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18130"/><hi type="bold">8. But--</hi>reverting to <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.4">1Ti 5:4</reference>, "If any (a general proposition; therefore including in its application the widow's children or grandchildren) provide not for his own (relations in general), and especially for those of his own house (in particular), he hath (practically) denied the faith." Faith without love and its works is dead; "for the subject matter of faith is not mere opinion, but the grace and truth of God, to which he that believes gives up his spirit, as he that loves gives up his heart" [Mack]. If in any case a duty of love is plain, it is in relation to one's own relatives; to fail in so plain an obligation is a plain proof of want of love, and therefore of want of faith. "Faith does not set aside natural duties, but strengthens them" [Bengel].<div eID="gen37359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37360" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">worse than an infidel--</hi>because even an infidel (or unbeliever) is taught by nature to provide for his own relatives, and generally recognizes the duty; the Christian who does not so, is worse (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.46">Mt 5:46</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.47">47</reference>). He has less excuse with his greater light than the infidel who may break the laws of nature. <div eID="gen37360" type="x-p"/>
entries.57e2871be0223db55d1f901fcf7e532558af66e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18131"/><div sID="gen37361" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18131"/>9. Translate, "As a widow (that is, of the ecclesiastical order of widowhood; a kind of female presbytery), let none be enrolled (in the catalogue) who is less than sixty years old." These were not deaconesses, who were chosen at a younger age (forty was the age fixed at the Council of Chalcedon), and who had virgins (in a later age called widows) as well as widows among them, but a band of widows set apart, though not yet formally and finally, to the service of God and the Church. Traces of such a class appear in <reference osisRef="Acts.9.41">Ac 9:41</reference>. Dorcas herself was such a one. As it was expedient (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.2">1Ti 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.6">Tit 1:6</reference>) that the presbyter or bishop should have been but once married, so also in her case. There is a transition here to a new subject. The reference here cannot be, as in <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.3">1Ti 5:3</reference>, to providing Church sustenance for them. For the restriction to widows above sixty would then be needless and harsh, since many widows might be in need of help at a much earlier age; as also the rule that the widow must not have been twice married, especially since he himself, below (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.14">1Ti 5:14</reference>) enjoins the younger widows to marry again; as also that she must have brought up children. Moreover, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.10">1Ti 5:10</reference> presupposes some competence, at least in past times, and so poor widows would be excluded, the very class requiring charity. Also, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.11">1Ti 5:11</reference> would then be senseless, for then their remarrying would be a benefit, not an injury, to the Church, as relieving it of the burden of their sustenance. Tertullian [On the Veiling of Virgins, 9], Hermas [Shepherd, 1.2], and Chrysostom [Homily, 31], mention such an order of ecclesiastical widowhood, each one not less than sixty years old, and resembling the presbyters in the respect paid to them, and in some of their duties; they ministered with sympathizing counsel to other widows and to orphans, a ministry to which their own experimental knowledge of the feelings and sufferings of the bereaved adapted them, and had a general supervision of their sex. Age was doubtless a requisite in presbyters, as it is here stated to have been in presbyteresses, with a view to their influence on the younger persons of their sex They were supported by the Church, but not the only widows so supported (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.3">1Ti 5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen37361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37362" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wife of one man--</hi>in order not to throw a stumbling-block in the way of Jews and heathen, who regarded with disfavor second marriages (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.2">1Ti 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.6">Tit 1:6</reference>). This is the force of "blameless," giving no offense, even in matters indifferent. <div eID="gen37362" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d9343b795ff8493e2a5a9a95e3ccc3cec9393a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18132"/><div sID="gen37363" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18132"/><hi type="bold">10. for good works--</hi>Greek, "IN honourable (excellent) works"; the sphere or element in which the good report of her had place (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.7">Tit 2:7</reference>). This answers to <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.7">1Ti 3:7</reference>, as to the bishop or presbyter, "He must have a good report of them which are without."<div eID="gen37363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37364" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if--</hi>if, in addition to being "well reported of."<div eID="gen37364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37365" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">she ... brought up children--</hi>either her own (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.4">1Ti 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.12">12</reference>), or those of others, which is one of the "good works"; a qualification adapting her for ministry to orphan children, and to mothers of families.<div eID="gen37365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37366" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lodged strangers--</hi><reference osisRef="1Tim.3.2">1Ti 3:2</reference>, "given to hospitality" (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.8">Tit 1:8</reference>); in the case of presbyters.<div eID="gen37366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">washed ... saints' feet--</hi>after the example of the Lord (<reference osisRef="John.13.14">Joh 13:14</reference>); a specimen of the universal spirit of humbly "by love serving one another," which actuated the early Christians.<div eID="gen37367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37368" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">relieved the afflicted--</hi>whether by pecuniary or other relief.<div eID="gen37368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">followed ... good--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.15">1Th 5:15</reference>; compare instances in <reference osisRef="Matt.25.35">Mt 25:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.36">36</reference>). <div eID="gen37369" type="x-p"/>
entries.4529f2d445c5fc349048c142cf39a1fd5b13782a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18133"/><div sID="gen37370" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18133"/><hi type="bold">11. younger--</hi>than sixty years old (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.9">1Ti 5:9</reference>).<div eID="gen37370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37371" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">refuse--</hi>to take on the roll of presbyteress widows.<div eID="gen37371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wax wanton--</hi>literally, "over-strong" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.26.16">2Ch 26:16</reference>).<div eID="gen37372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37373" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against Christ--</hi>rebelling against Christ, their proper Bridegroom [Jerome].<div eID="gen37373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37374" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they will--</hi>Greek, "they wish"; their desire is to marry again. <div eID="gen37374" type="x-p"/>
entries.489776fc36d1a9ca3811d040545e741116fdfe71: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18134"/><div sID="gen37375" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18134"/><hi type="bold">12. Having--</hi>Bringing on themselves, and so having to bear as a burden (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.10">Ga 5:10</reference>) judgment from God (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.6">1Ti 3:6</reference>), weighing like a load on them.<div eID="gen37375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37376" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast off their first faith--</hi>namely, pledged to Christ and the service of the Church. There could be no hardship at the age of sixty or upwards in not marrying again (end of <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.9">1Ti 5:9</reference>), for the sake of serving better the cause of Christ as presbyteresses; though, to ordinary widows, no barrier existed against remarriage (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.39">1Co 7:39</reference>). This is altogether distinct from Rome's unnatural vows of celibacy in the case of young marriageable women. The widow-presbyteresses, moreover, engaged to remain single, not as though single life were holier than married life (according to Rome's teaching), but because the interests of Christ's cause made it desirable (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.2">1Ti 3:2</reference>). They had pledged "their first faith" to Christ as presbyteress widows; they now wish to transfer their faith to a husband (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.32">1Co 7:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.34">34</reference>). <div eID="gen37376" type="x-p"/>
entries.934bb6a2cc349eae74e91a627e2288bc768a33a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18135"/><div sID="gen37377" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18135"/><hi type="bold">13. withal--</hi>"at the same time, moreover."<div eID="gen37377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37378" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">learn--</hi>usually in a good sense. But these women's "learning" is idleness, trifling, and busybodies' tattle.<div eID="gen37378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37379" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wandering--</hi>Greek, "going about."<div eID="gen37379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37380" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from house to house--</hi>of the members of the Church (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.6">2Ti 3:6</reference>). "They carry the affairs of this house to that, and of that to this; they tell the affairs of all to all" [Theophylact].<div eID="gen37380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37381" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tattlers--</hi>literally "trifling talkers." In 3Jo 10, translated "prating."<div eID="gen37381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37382" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">busybodies--</hi>mischievously busy; inconsiderately curious (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.11">2Th 3:11</reference>). <reference osisRef="Acts.19.19">Ac 19:19</reference>, "curious," the same Greek. Curiosity usually springs from idleness, which is itself the mother of garrulity [Calvin].<div eID="gen37382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37383" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speaking--</hi>not merely "saying." The subject-matter, as well as the form, is involved in the Greek word [Alford].<div eID="gen37383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37384" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which they ought not--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Titus.1.11">Tit 1:11</reference>). <div eID="gen37384" type="x-p"/>
entries.64580c1d52f2afb5c55de66d575a763857af2092: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18136"/><div sID="gen37385" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18136"/><hi type="bold">14. younger women--</hi>rather, as ellipsis ought to be supplied, "the younger widows," namely younger widows in general, as distinguished from the older widows taken on the roll of presbyteresses (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.9">1Ti 5:9</reference>). The "therefore" means seeing that young widows are exposed to such temptations, "I will," or "desire," &c. (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.11-1Tim.5.13">1Ti 5:11-13</reference>). The precept here that they should marry again is not inconsistent with <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.40">1Co 7:40</reference>; for the circumstances of the two cases were distinct (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.26">1Co 7:26</reference>). Here remarriage is recommended as an antidote to sexual passion, idleness, and the other evils noted in <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.11-1Tim.5.13">1Ti 5:11-13</reference>. Of course, where there was no tendency to these evils, marriage again would not be so requisite; Paul speaks of what is generally desirable, and supposing there should be danger of such evils, as was likely. "He does not impose a law, but points out a remedy, to younger widows" [Chrysostom].<div eID="gen37385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37386" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bear children--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.15">1Ti 2:15</reference>); thus gaining one of the qualifications (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.10">1Ti 5:10</reference>) for being afterwards a presbyteress widow, should Providence so ordain it.<div eID="gen37386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37387" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">guide--</hi>Greek, "rule the house" in the woman's due place; not usurping authority over the man (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.12">1Ti 2:12</reference>).<div eID="gen37387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">give none occasion--</hi>literally, "starting-point": handle of reproach through the loose conduct of nominal Christians.<div eID="gen37388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the adversary--</hi>of Christianity, Jew or Gentile. <reference osisRef="Phil.1.28">Php 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.8">Tit 2:8</reference>, "He that is of the contrary part." Not Satan, who is introduced in a different relation (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.15">1Ti 5:15</reference>).<div eID="gen37389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to speak reproachfully--</hi>literally, "for the sake of reproach" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.7">1Ti 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.1">6:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.5">Tit 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">10</reference>). If the handle were given, the adversary would use it for the sake of reproach. The adversary is eager to exaggerate the faults of a few, and to lay the blame on the whole Church and its doctrines [Bengel]. <div eID="gen37390" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab10f01a3ee1f849e8bedfd1b7f18ddcdff77e11: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18137"/><div sID="gen37391" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18137"/><hi type="bold">15. For--</hi>For in the case of some this result has already ensued; "Some (widows) are already turned aside after Satan," the seducer (not by falling away from the faith in general, but) by such errors as are stigmatized in <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.11-1Tim.5.13">1Ti 5:11-13</reference>, sexual passion, idleness, &c., and so have given occasion of reproach (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.14">1Ti 5:14</reference>). "Satan finds some mischief still for the idle hands to do." <div eID="gen37391" type="x-p"/>
entries.af9e4950d1cbe32ff851598e8230ec29922d47bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18138"/><div sID="gen37392" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18138"/><hi type="bold">16. If any ... have widows--</hi>of his family, however related to him. Most of the oldest manuscripts and versions omit "man or," and read, "If any woman that believeth." But the Received text seems preferable. If, however, the weightiest authorities are to prevail, the sense will be: He was speaking of younger widows; He now says, If any believing young widow have widows related to her needing support, let her relieve them, thereby casing the Church of the burden, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.3">1Ti 5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.4">4</reference> (there it was the children and grandchildren; here it is the young widow, who, in order to avoid the evils of idleness and wantonness, the result of idleness, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.11">1Ti 5:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.49">Eze 16:49</reference>, is to be diligent in good works, such as "relieving the afflicted," <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.10">1Ti 5:10</reference>, thus qualifying herself for being afterwards a widow-presbyteress).<div eID="gen37392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37393" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let them--</hi>rather as Greek, "let him," or "her"; "let such a one" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.10">1Ti 5:10</reference>).<div eID="gen37393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37394" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be charged--</hi>literally, "be burdened" with their support.<div eID="gen37394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37395" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">widows indeed--</hi>really helpless and friendless (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.3">1Ti 5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.4">4</reference>). <div eID="gen37395" type="x-p"/>
entries.b999b934957f887e5d279fdef3e49c20164dbb3c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18139"/><div sID="gen37396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18139"/>17. The transition from the widow presbyteresses (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.9">1Ti 5:9</reference>) to the presbyters here, is natural.<div eID="gen37396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37397" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rule well--</hi>literally, "preside well," with wisdom, ability, and loving faithfulness, over the flock assigned to them.<div eID="gen37397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37398" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be counted worthy of double honour--</hi>that is, the honor which is expressed by gifts (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.3">1Ti 5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.18">18</reference>) and otherwise. If a presbyter as such, in virtue of his office, is already worthy of honor, he who rules well is doubly so [Wiesinger] (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.14">1Co 9:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.6">Ga 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.12">1Th 5:12</reference>). Not literally that a presbyter who rules well should get double the salary of one who does not rule well [Alford], or of a presbyteress widow, or of the deacons [Chrysostom]. "Double" is used for large in general (<reference osisRef="Rev.18.6">Re 18:6</reference>).<div eID="gen37398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37399" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">specially they who labour in the word and doctrine--</hi>Greek, "teaching"; preaching of the word, and instruction, catechetical or otherwise. This implies that of the ruling presbyters there were two kinds, those who labored in the word and teaching, and those who did not. Lay presbyters, so called merely because of their age, have no place here; for both classes mentioned here alike are ruling presbyters. A college of presbyters is implied as existing in each large congregation. As in <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.1-1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:1-16</reference> their qualifications are spoken of, so here the acknowledgments due to them for their services. <div eID="gen37399" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a45cb1ae55a88454b38e0fcd63e8771d42b0ce0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18140"/><div sID="gen37400" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18140"/><hi type="bold">18. the scripture--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.25.4">De 25:4</reference>; quoted before in <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.9">1Co 9:9</reference>).<div eID="gen37400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37401" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the ox that treadeth out--</hi>Greek, An ox while treading.<div eID="gen37401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37402" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The labourer is worthy of his reward--</hi>or "hire"; quoted from <reference osisRef="Luke.10.7">Lu 10:7</reference>, whereas <reference osisRef="Matt.10.10">Mt 10:10</reference> has "his meat," or "food." If Paul extends the phrase, "Scripture saith," to this second clause, as well as to the first, he will be hereby recognizing the Gospel of Luke, his own helper (whence appears the undesigned appositeness of the quotation), as inspired Scripture. This I think the correct view. The Gospel according to Luke was probably in circulation then about eight or nine years. However, it is possible "Scripture saith" applies only to the passage quoted from <reference osisRef="Deut.25.4">De 25:4</reference>; and then his quotation will be that of a common proverb, quoted also by the Lord, which commends itself to the approval of all, and is approved by the Lord and His apostle. <div eID="gen37402" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f512942612dc29e8f75df0d1cd199ffa2bb2027: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18141"/><div sID="gen37403" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18141"/><hi type="bold">19. Against an elder--</hi>a presbyter of the Church.<div eID="gen37403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">receive not--</hi>"entertain not" [Alford].<div eID="gen37404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37405" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but before two or three witnesses--</hi>A judicial conviction was not permitted in <reference osisRef="Deut.17.6">De 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.19.15">19:15</reference>, except on the testimony of at least two or three witnesses (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.18.16">Mt 18:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.17">Joh 8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.1">2Co 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.6">1Jo 5:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.5.7">7</reference>). But Timothy's entertaining an accusation against anyone is a different case, where the object was not judicially to punish, but to admonish: here he might ordinarily entertain it without the need of two or three witnesses; but not in the case of an elder, since the more earnest an elder was to convince gainsayers (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.9">Tit 1:9</reference>), the more exposed would he be to vexatious and false accusations. How important then was it that Timothy should not, without strong testimony, entertain a charge against presbyters, who should, in order to be efficient, be "blameless" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.2">1Ti 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.6">Tit 1:6</reference>). <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.21">1Ti 5:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.24">24</reference> imply that Timothy had the power of judging in the Church. Doubtless he would not condemn any save on the testimony of two or three witnesses, but in ordinary cases he would cite them, as the law of Moses also allowed, though there were only one witness. But in the case of elders, he would require two or three witnesses before even citing them; for their character for innocence stands higher, and they are exposed to envy and calumny more than others "Receive" does not, as Alford thinks, include both citation and conviction, but means only the former. <div eID="gen37405" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0bbaca167fea9c8c6a790215b3b5221c745a07b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18142"/><div sID="gen37406" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18142"/><hi type="bold">20. Them that sin--</hi>whether presbyters or laymen.<div eID="gen37406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37407" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rebuke before all--</hi>publicly before the Church (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.15-Matt.18.17">Mt 18:15-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.9-1Cor.5.13">1Co 5:9-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.11">Ep 5:11</reference>). Not until this "rebuke" was disregarded was the offender to be excommunicated.<div eID="gen37407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37408" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">others ... fear--</hi>that other members of the Church may have a wholesome fear of offending (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.11">De 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.5.11">Ac 5:11</reference>). <div eID="gen37408" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fc44f3715d7b32a52ff291c0fff2c682eacd4ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18143"/><div sID="gen37409" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18143"/><hi type="bold">21. I charge thee--</hi>rather as Greek, "I adjure thee"; so it ought to be translated (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.1">2Ti 4:1</reference>).<div eID="gen37409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37410" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before--</hi>"in the presence of God."<div eID="gen37410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37411" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts God the Father, and Christ the Son, will testify against thee, if thou disregardest my injunction. He vividly sets before Timothy the last judgment, in which God shall be revealed, and Christ seen face to face with His angels<div eID="gen37411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37412" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">elect angels--</hi>an epithet of reverence. The objects of divine electing love (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.6">1Pe 2:6</reference>). Not only "elect" (according to the everlasting purpose of God) in contradistinction to the reprobate angels (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.4">2Pe 2:4</reference>), but also to mark the excellence of the angels in general (as God's chosen ministers, "holy angels," "angels of light"), and so to give more solemnity to their testimony [Calvin] as witnesses to Paul's adjuration. Angels take part by action and sympathy in the affairs of the earth (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.10">Lu 15:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">1Co 4:9</reference>).<div eID="gen37412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37413" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">these things--</hi>the injunctions, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.19">1Ti 5:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.20">20</reference>.<div eID="gen37413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37414" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without preferring one before another--</hi>rather as Greek, "prejudice"; "judging before" hearing all the facts of a case. There ought to be judgment, but not prejudging. Compare "suddenly," <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.22">1Ti 5:22</reference>, also <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.24">1Ti 5:24</reference>.<div eID="gen37414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37415" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">partiality--</hi>in favor of a man, as "prejudice" is bias against a man. Some of the oldest manuscripts read, "in the way of summoning (brethren) before a (heathen) judge." But Vulgate and other good authorities favor the more probable reading in English Version. <div eID="gen37415" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf9cfc1edfe9e011cce26787c16e4281f9309823: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18144"/><div sID="gen37416" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18144"/><hi type="bold">22. Lay hands--</hi>that is, ordain (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.14">1Ti 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">2Ti 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.5">Tit 1:5</reference>). The connection is with <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.19">1Ti 5:19</reference>. The way to guard against scandals occurring in the case of presbyters is, be cautious as to the character of the candidate before ordaining him; this will apply to other Church officers so ordained, as well as to presbyters. Thus, this clause refers to <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.19">1Ti 5:19</reference>, as next clause, "neither be partaker of other men's sins," refers to <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.20">1Ti 5:20</reference>. Ellicott and Wiesinger understand it of receiving back into Church fellowship or absolution, by laying hands on those who had been "rebuked" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.20">1Ti 5:20</reference>) and then excommunicated (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.17">Mt 18:17</reference>); <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.20">1Ti 5:20</reference> favors this. But as in <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.14">1Ti 4:14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Acts.6.6">Ac 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.3">13:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">2Ti 1:6</reference>, the laying on of hands is used of ordination (compare however as to confirmation, <reference osisRef="Acts.8.17">Ac 8:17</reference>), it seems better to take it so here.<div eID="gen37416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37417" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">suddenly--</hi>hastily: <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.24">1Ti 5:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.25">25</reference> show that waiting for a time is salutary.<div eID="gen37417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37418" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither be partaker of other men's sins--</hi>by negligence in ordaining ungodly candidates, and so becoming in some degree responsible for their sins. Or, there is the same transition from the elders to all in general who may sin, as in <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.19">1Ti 5:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.20">20</reference>. Be not a partaker in other men's sins by not "rebuking them that sin before all," as well as those that are candidates for the presbytery, as also all "that sin."<div eID="gen37418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37419" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">keep thyself pure--</hi>"thyself' is emphatic. "Keep THYSELF" clear of participation in OTHER men's sin by not failing to rebuke them that sin (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.20">1Ti 5:20</reference>). Thus the transition is easy to <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.23">1Ti 5:23</reference>, which is concerning Timothy personally; compare also <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.24">1Ti 5:24</reference>. <div eID="gen37419" type="x-p"/>
entries.1937e66704b68700eb824b784c1c5d5f80fe8e96: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18145"/><div sID="gen37420" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18145"/><hi type="bold">23. no longer--</hi>as a habit. This injunction to drink wine occasionally is a modification of the preceding "keep thyself pure." The presbyter and deacon were enjoined to be "not given to wine" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.3">1Ti 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.8">8</reference>). Timothy seems to have had a tendency to undue ascetical strictness on this point (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">1Ti 4:8</reference>; compare the Nazarene vow, <reference osisRef="Num.6.1-Num.6.4">Nu 6:1-4</reference>; John the Baptist, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.15">Lu 1:15</reference>; Ro 14). Paul therefore modifies the preceding words, "keep thyself pure," virtually saying, "Not that I mean to enjoin that kind of purity which consists in asceticism, nay, be no longer a water-drinker," that is, no longer drink only water, but use a little wine, as much as is needed for thy health. So Ellicott and Wiesinger. Alford thus: Timothy was of a feeble frame (see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.10">1Co 16:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.11">11</reference>), and prone to timidity in his duties as overseer where vigorous action was needed; hence Paul exhorts him to take all proper means to raise his bodily condition above these infirmities. God hereby commands believers to use all due means for preserving health, and condemns by anticipation the human traditions which among various sects have denied the use of wine to the faithful. <div eID="gen37420" type="x-p"/>
entries.29eaeadc2bad10834d3d2fd1a3824cf93ed396e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18146"/><div sID="gen37421" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18146"/>24. Two kinds of sins are specified: those palpably manifest (so the Greek for "open beforehand" ought to be translated; so in <reference osisRef="Heb.7.14">He 7:14</reference>, it is translated "evident"; literally, "before" the eyes, that is, notorious), further explained as "going before to judgment"; and those which follow after the men ("some men they, that is, their sins, follow after"), namely, not going beforehand, loudly accusing, but hidden till they come to the judgment: so <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.25">1Ti 5:25</reference>, the good works are of two classes: those palpably manifest (translate so, instead of "manifest beforehand") and "those that are otherwise," that is, not palpably manifest. Both alike "cannot be hid"; the former class in the case of bad and good are manifest already; the latter class in the case of both are not manifest now, but shall be so at the final judgment.<div eID="gen37421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37422" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">going before to judgment--</hi>as heralds; crying sins which accuse their perpetrator. The connection seems to me this: He had enjoined Timothy, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.20">1Ti 5:20</reference>, "Rebuke them that sin before all": and in <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.22">1Ti 5:22</reference>, "Neither be partaker of other men's sins," by ordaining ungodly men; having then by a digression at the clause, "keep thyself pure," guarded against an ascetical error of Timothy in fancying purity consisted in asceticism, and having exhorted him to use wine for strengthening him in his work, he returns to the subject of his being vigorous as an overseer in rebuking sin, whether in presbyters or people, and in avoiding participation in men's sins by ordaining ungodly candidates. He says, therefore, there are two classes of sins, as there are two classes of good works: those palpably manifest, and those not so; the former are those on which thou shouldest act decidedly at once when called on, whether to rebuke in general, or to ordain ministers in particular; as to the latter, the final judgment alone can decide; however hidden now they "cannot be hid" then. This could only be said of the final judgment (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">1Co 4:5</reference>; therefore, Alford's reference of this verse to Timothy's judgment in choosing elders must be wrong); all judgments before then are fallible. Thus he implies that Timothy can only be responsible if he connive at manifest, or evident sins; not that those that are otherwise shall escape judgment at last: just as in the case of good works, he can only be responsible for taking into account in his judgments those which are patent to all, not those secret good works which nevertheless will not remain hidden at the final judgment. <chapter eID="1Tim.5"/>

entries.3aa6d590ecf4618a1171037ada7739609323d856: <div eID="gen51767" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen51768" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51769" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51769" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51768" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51770" type="x-p"/> Rules to be observed in giving reproofs to the old and to the young, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.1">1Tim 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.2">1Tim 5:2</reference>. Directions concerning widows, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.3-1Tim.5.16">1Tim 5:3-16</reference>. Of elders that rule well, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17">1Tim 5:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.18">1Tim 5:18</reference>. How to proceed against elders when accused, and against notorious offenders, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.10-1Tim.5.21">1Tim 5:10-21</reference>. Directions concerning imposition of hands, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.22">1Tim 5:22</reference>. Concerning Timothy's health, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.23">1Tim 5:23</reference>. Reasons why no person should be hastily appointed to sacred offices, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.24">1Tim 5:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.25">1Tim 5:25</reference>. <div eID="gen51770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51771" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen51771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51772" type="x-p"/> Rebuke not an elder - That is, an elderly person; for the word πρεσβυτερος is here taken in its natural sense, and signifies one advanced in years. At <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17">1Tim 5:17</reference>, it is taken in what may be termed its ecclesiastical meaning, and signifies, an officer in the Church, what we commonly call a presbyter or bishop; for sometimes these terms were confounded. There are but few cases in which it at all becomes a young man to reprove an old man, and especially one who is a father in the Church. If such a one does wrong, or gets out of the way, he should be entreated as a father, with great caution and respect. To this at least his age entitles him. The word επιπληξῃς signifies, do not smite; i.e. do not treat them harshly, nor with magisterial austerity. <div eID="gen51772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51773" type="x-p"/> The younger men as brethren - Showing humility, and arrogating nothing to thyself on account of thy office. Feel for them as thou oughtest to feel for thy own brethren.
entries.df41332448809fa99283e80813909f5cfa367503: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen51773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51774" type="x-p"/> The elder women as mothers - Treating them with the respect due to their age. <div eID="gen51774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51775" type="x-p"/> The younger as sisters - Feel for every member of the Church, old and young, male and female; consider them as fathers, mothers, brothers, and sisters; treat them all with gentleness; and labor to keep them in, not to expel them from, the Church. <div eID="gen51775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51776" type="x-p"/> With all purity - Εν πασῃ ἁγνειᾳ· With all chastity. See the note on <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Tim 4:12</reference>. <div eID="gen51776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51777" type="x-p"/> There are some who seem to take a barbarous pleasure in expelling members from, the Church. They should be continued in as long as possible; while they are in the Church - under its ordinances and discipline, there is some hope that their errors may be corrected; but when once driven out again into the world, that hope must necessarily become extinct. As judgment is God's strange work, so excommunication should be the strange, the last, and the most reluctantly performed work of every Christian minister.
entries.0091062dcdcbd4a86f84dacc95e9f0712d67b815: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen51777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51778" type="x-p"/> Honor widows that are widows indeed - One meaning of the word τιμαω, to honor, is to support, sustain, etc., <reference osisRef="Mat.15.4">Mat 15:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.15.5">Mat 15:5</reference>; and here it is most obviously to be taken in this sense. Provide for those widows especially which are widows indeed - persons truly destitute, being aged and helpless, and having neither children nor friends to take care of them, and who behave as becometh their destitute state. But see the note on <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.10">1Tim 5:10</reference>.
entries.f5234079a268fe340ebf37b5d8692bd5689d7b1c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen51778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51779" type="x-p"/> But if any widow have children or nephews - This shows that widows indeed are those that have neither children nor nephews, i.e. no relatives that either will or can help them, or no near relatives alive. <div eID="gen51779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51780" type="x-p"/> Let them learn first to show piety at home - Let these children and nephews provide for their aged or helpless parents or relatives, and not burden the Church with them while they are able to support them. <div eID="gen51780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51781" type="x-p"/> And to requite their parents - Και αμοιβας αποδιδοναι τοις προγονοις· Let them learn to give benefit for benefit. Your parents supported and nourished you when you were young and helpless; you ought therefore to support them when they are old and destitute. This is called showing piety; and there is doubtless an allusion to the fifth commandment: Honour thy father and thy mother - provide for them in their old age and afflictions; God commands this.
entries.075740d6c6d654a19754a8f33510c02dcd9a3a15: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen51781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51782" type="x-p"/> And desolate - Και μεμονωμενη· Left entirely alone - having neither children nor relatives to take care of her. <div eID="gen51782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51783" type="x-p"/> Trusteth in God - Finding she has no other helper, she continues in prayer and supplication, that she may derive that from God which, in the course of his providence, he has deprived her of among men.
entries.3e6afe54dbee760c45d087905f83b62b52305aa4: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen51783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51784" type="x-p"/> But she that liveth in pleasure - Ἡ δε σπαταλωσα· She that liveth delicately - voluptuously indulging herself with dainties; it does not indicate grossly criminal pleasures; but simply means one who indulges herself in good eating and drinking, pampering her body at the expense of her mind. The word is used in reference to what we term petted and spoiled children; and a remarkable passage, is produced by Kypke, from an epistle of Theanus to Eubulus, found in Opusc. Myth. Galaei, page 741, where he says: "What can be done with that boy, who, if he have not food when and as he pleases, bursts out into weeping; and, if he eats, must have dainties and sweetmeats? If the weather be hot he complains of fatigue; if it be cold, he trembles; if he be reproved, he scolds; if every thing be not provided for him according to his wish, he is enraged.
